newsitem.title: PERU: Mourners cry for vengeance at Peru guerrilla burial.
newsitem.headline: Mourners cry for vengeance at Peru guerrilla burial.

text.p: With shouts for vengeance echoing through a dusty shantytown cemetery, comrades and relatives of Marxist rebel Rolly Rojas buried him on Thursday in a hastily prepared grave near the jail where he was once imprisoned.

Mourners carried his rough wooden coffin through the graveyard in Lima's San Juan de Lurigancho district and slid it into an above-ground niche, the way most Peruvians are buried, while his mother and other relatives wept.
"Vengeance!" and "Long live MRTA!" mourners shouted during the night-time funeral, illuminated only by five candles and the harsh glare of a few television spotlights.
"It was a poor man's box," said one old woman at the funeral, describing the rough wooden coffin carrying Rojas, who died at age 34.

For Rojas, known as "The Arab" to his comrades in the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA), the poverty of his burial matched the poverty of his life in the tough neighbourhood on Lima's northern flank.

One of the first Lima districts where MRTA tried to win over young converts in the early 1980s, San Juan de Lurigancho is a collection of adobe homes, many with no power or water, and shantytowns scratched into the surrounding hillsides.
It is home to the notorious Lurigancho prison and the top- security Canto Grande prison, where Rojas and several other captured MRTA rebels were kept before escaping in 1990.
Some residents ventured out of their makeshift houses, while others more afraid kept a watchful eye from within their house as police jeeps packed with uneasy-looking policemen kept watch.
There were almost as many policemen as mourners, who numbered about 30.
"I am the mother of Rolly Rojas Fernandez. Rolly didn't deserve this. It hurts me so much what they did to my son. Why, why? He was a very good person," Maria Rojas sobbed.

"He negotiated a lot, with everybody. He even negotiated with the president (Alberto Fujimori) himself. The president himself said to him, 'You can talk,'" she said, referring to her son's role in the failed negotiations to end the siege peacefully.

For a man who died a Marxist, the burial site could hardly have been more appropriate. It was in an unregistered, "informal" graveyard like those that spring up at all Peruvian slums, where residents with no money to bury their dead in more respectable sites can pay a fee, look for a vacant niche and seal it up with cement.
In the fresh cement enveloping Rojas' cheap coffin, someone etched his name and a cross.
